lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Part 2. You will hear the volunteer coordinator of a science festival speaking on a podcast. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: Hello, and welcome to the Westbay Science Festival podcast. I'm Kate Lowe, and I look after the festival's team of volunteers.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: The festival runs for ten days every September, and each year we need around three hundred volunteers to keep everything running smoothly.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: If you're thinking of joining us, I'd like to start by reading you a message from Priya, a university student who has volunteered with us for the last two years.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: Priya writes: 'In my first year, I was put in the Nature Tent, which was great fun, although it rained almost every day. I also spent a few afternoons in the Kitchen Lab, where children make ice cream and fizzy drinks and learn the chemistry behind them.'

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: 'I enjoyed the Kitchen Lab so much that I asked to go back there last year, and luckily they said yes.'

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: 'Last year I also did several shifts on the Information Desk. I was nervous at first, but answering visitors' questions all day really built up my confidence.'

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: 'This year, I'm hoping to be in the Robot Garage, because I'm studying engineering. And one day I'd love to help with the shows in the Space Dome, but you need special training for that.'

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: Thanks, Priya. We'll see what we can do!

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: Now, people often ask what volunteers get in return for their time. Apart from a festival T-shirt and a free lunch on the days you work, every volunteer receives a travel pass.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: The pass gives you free travel on all the city's buses, and it also covers the ferries that cross the bay. That's very handy, because several of our venues are on the north shore.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: Some people assume the pass is only valid on the days they're actually volunteering, but that isn't the case. You can use it every day from the opening morning until the closing night, so you can come and enjoy the events yourself when you're off duty.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: After the closing night, though, it stops working, so don't try to use it the following week!

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: I'm afraid the pass has your photo on it, so it can't be lent to friends or members of your family.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: And you won't need to queue up for it at the festival office. We'll post it to your home address about a fortnight before the festival begins.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the podcast, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: Every evening during the festival there's a talk in the City Hall by a guest speaker, and volunteers get free tickets. So let me tell you who's coming this year.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: Our first speaker is Dr Ruth Okafor. Ruth began her career as a chemistry teacher, before moving into climate research.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: Since then she has spent two winters at a research station in Antarctica, and several months in one of the driest deserts on Earth. Her talk is about what daily life and work are really like in places where the conditions are so harsh.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: Next is Marcus Bell, who many of you will know from his television series about wildlife. But this time he won't be talking about animals.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: Instead, he'll be showing how big scientific ideas can be explained with ordinary things you'd find in any kitchen drawer, like spoons, balloons and elastic bands.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: Then we have Hannah Price. Hannah trained as an engineer and spent ten years designing machines for farms.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: These days she works for the city council, and her talk will be about how we can make our towns safer places for birds, bats and insects, for example by planting gardens on roofs.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: Leo Martins is a physicist who is well known for his work on solar power. He's won several prizes, but that's not what he'll be discussing.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: He'll be talking about his very first major project, a machine that took him three years to build and then never worked, and what that disappointment taught him.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: Sofia Andersen's photographs of insects have appeared in magazines all over the world.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: But until she was forty, photography was just something she did at weekends while she worked in a bank. Her talk explains how she managed to make a living from her favourite pastime.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: And finally, Amir Haddad. Amir grew up on a farm, and he's been fascinated by machines and computers since he was a boy.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: He now designs museum exhibits that people who are blind or partially sighted can explore through touch and sound, and that's the work he'll be focusing on.

lines.speaker: KATE
lines.text: So, if you'd like to apply, the form is on our website, and the closing date is the end of June.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: That is the end of Part 2.

groups.stem: In which TWO areas of the festival did Priya work last year?
Which TWO facts are given about the volunteers' travel pass?

options.text: It covers more than one type of public transport.
It can still be used for a week after the festival ends.
It is only valid on the days a volunteer is working.
Members of a volunteer's family may also use it.
It will be delivered to volunteers' homes.

groups.instructions: What will each of the following speakers talk about? Choose SIX answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–G, next to Questions 15–20.
groups.title: Topics

options.text: making science accessible to people with disabilities
what can be learned from an unsuccessful project
using everyday objects to explain science
turning a hobby into a career

evidence.quote: I asked to go back there last year

pairs: Last year I also did several shifts on the Information Desk
11.why: Priya worked in the Kitchen Lab in her first year and went back there last year (B). Last year she also worked on the Information Desk (D).
11.trap: A and C are where she hopes to work in the future, not last year. E, the Nature Tent, was only in her first year.

evidence.quote: Last year I also did several shifts on the Information Desk

pairs: Last year I also did several shifts on the Information Desk
12.why: The two correct answers are B and D, in either order. Listen for 'last year' to separate them from her first year and her hopes for this year.
12.trap: A and C are where she hopes to work in the future, not last year. E, the Nature Tent, was only in her first year.

evidence.quote: free travel on all the city's buses, and it also covers the ferries

pairs: more than one type of public transport
buses … and it also covers the ferries
We'll post it to your home address
13.why: The pass works on buses and on ferries, so it covers more than one type of transport (A). It will be posted to volunteers' home addresses (E).
13.trap: B is wrong: the pass stops working after the closing night. C is wrong: Kate says it is valid every day of the festival, not only working days. D is wrong: it has your photo on it and can't be lent to family.

evidence.quote: We'll post it to your home address

pairs: more than one type of public transport
buses … and it also covers the ferries
We'll post it to your home address
14.why: The two correct answers are A and E, in either order. 'Post it to your home address' means it will be delivered to your home.
14.trap: B is wrong: the pass stops working after the closing night. C is wrong: Kate says it is valid every day of the festival, not only working days. D is wrong: it has your photo on it and can't be lent to family.

evidence.quote: Her talk is about what daily life and work are really like in places where the conditions are so harsh

pairs: daily life and work … in places where the conditions are so harsh
15.why: Ruth has worked in Antarctica and a very dry desert. Places with harsh conditions are extreme environments.
15.trap: She was once a chemistry teacher, but teaching is not what her talk is about.

evidence.quote: ordinary things you'd find in any kitchen drawer

pairs: ordinary things you'd find in any kitchen drawer
how big scientific ideas can be explained
16.why: Marcus will explain scientific ideas with spoons, balloons and elastic bands. These are everyday objects.
16.trap: He is famous for a wildlife series, but Kate says 'this time he won't be talking about animals', so G is wrong.

evidence.quote: how we can make our towns safer places for birds, bats and insects

pairs: safer places for birds, bats and insects
17.why: Hannah's talk is about making towns safer for birds, bats and insects. Towns are urban areas, and these animals are wildlife.
17.trap: She used to design farm machines, which links to F. But that was her old job, not her talk.

evidence.quote: a machine that took him three years to build and then never worked, and what that disappointment taught him

18.why: Leo's first big project failed: the machine never worked. He will talk about what he learned from it.
18.trap: His prizes and solar power work are mentioned, but Kate says 'that's not what he'll be discussing'.

evidence.quote: how she managed to make a living from her favourite pastime

pairs: something she did at weekends … her favourite pastime
19.why: Photography was a weekend activity, a hobby. Her talk is about how she started earning money from it, so it became her career.
19.trap: Her photos are of insects, which may make you think of G (wildlife). But her talk is about her career change.

evidence.quote: people who are blind or partially sighted can explore through touch and sound

pairs: people who are blind or partially sighted
can explore through touch and sound
20.why: Amir designs museum exhibits that blind people can use by touch and sound. This makes science accessible to people with a disability.
20.trap: He grew up on a farm and loves machines and computers, which links to F. But F is not his topic.
